narrative.text: A pull quote stating that small, timely investments through the fund can save lives and cut the costs of responding to outbreaks and emergencies.
Lists the 13 countries that contributed to the Contingency Fund for Emergencies in 2020.

Explains that the Contingency Fund for Emergencies was set up in 2015 to let WHO deploy resources quickly before other funding mechanisms such as CERF are available, releasing funds within 24 hours. It notes that releases cover response activities, staff and supplies and are subject to WHO financial rules and annual reporting.
A map and key showing the 14 emergencies and the global COVID-19 response supported by the fund in 2020, grouped as outbreaks, complex emergencies, natural disasters and a technological disaster.

Reports that in 2020 the fund supported responses to 14 emergencies in 13 countries plus COVID-19, releasing nearly US$ 44 million, with about 80% going to COVID-19 and to two Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Details 2020 fund expenditures, including bridging funding gaps in the protracted North Kivu Ebola response, US$ 5.3 million for the Equateur Ebola outbreak and US$ 12.9 million for early COVID-19 response. It lists other emergencies supported, reports that most small allocations were released within 24 hours, and gives a table of releases by event and a chart of refund rates by year.

Explains that the fund was designed to be revolving but has been hard to replenish, with about 40% of 2020 allocations refunded. It notes that refunds vary by emergency, with most COVID-19 releases reimbursed but Ebola releases less so, and presents a table of releases and refunds by event.

Reports that 13 Member States contributed nearly US$ 23 million in 2020, down from previous years likely because of the focus on funding COVID-19, with Austria joining for the first time. Tables and a chart show contributions by country and for 2015–2020, and the block notes how the fund enabled rapid responses amid multiple crises.

Gives examples of rapid responses enabled by the fund, including over US$ 2 million released within 24 hours after the Beirut port explosion, support for the Equateur Ebola response, airlifted supplies in Syria, and cyclone response in Vanuatu. It notes support for COVID-19 supply chains and argues that small, early releases had outsized impact. The block also describes WHO's work in Lebanon on medicines, dialysis supplies and a mental health hotline.

Describes how WHO's Beirut response continued through a health coordination mechanism, with CERF and European Commission funds complementing the fund. It then introduces the Tropical Cyclone Harold response in Vanuatu, outlining initial assessment and priority activities to maintain health services and limit disease risks.

Describes WHO support in Vanuatu after Cyclone Harold despite COVID-19 restrictions, including emergency medical team deployment, surveillance tools and repairs to three health facilities, later reimbursed by CERF. It then outlines the health crisis in north-eastern Syria after displacement in 2019, where few health centres were fully functional and WHO used the fund to airlift supplies when borders closed.

Shows how fund support helped deliver supplies to partners in north-eastern Syria, then introduces the 11th Ebola outbreak in Equateur Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, which ended in November 2020 with 119 confirmed cases and 55 deaths. It notes the added strain of COVID-19 and the decentralised, community-based response.

Tells the story of community resistance to Ebola in Mbandaka, where youth leaders persuaded people to accept treatment and vaccination, and describes ultra-cold freezers used to vaccinate in areas without electricity. It credits the fund with launching and sustaining the response and calls for continued vigilance. The block ends with the start of the COVID-19 supply chain section, describing pandemic supply networks supported by early fund releases.

Describes how early Contingency Fund for Emergencies releases helped WHO build the COVID-19 supply chain system, including national planning support, supply catalogues, demand management, pooled procurement and stockpiling, and logistics through the World Food Programme. It presents this pooled, equitable approach as a lasting shift in pandemic preparedness and calls for sustainable financing of WHO, with the fund as a key part of emergency response.
Closes the 2020 fund report by urging that resource mobilisation for the fund be part of wider discussions on sustainable WHO financing and emergency preparedness.
Annex 1, a table of every approved fund release in 2020 by country, region, emergency type, amount and date, totalling about US$ 43.8 million.
A footnote to the releases table noting that the Nagorno-Karabakh regional release covered Armenia and Azerbaijan.
Annex 2, a table of fund utilisation by expenditure category as of April 2021, such as contractual services, staff agreements, supplies and travel, totalling about US$ 25 million.
Annex 3, a table of contributions to the fund by country for 2015–2020, led by Germany, Japan and the United Kingdom and totalling about US$ 159 million, followed by WHO contact details.

The front matter of WHO's 2020 annual report on the Contingency Fund for Emergencies (June 2021), with the copyright and licence page, contents and a foreword by the Director-General calling for continued support for flexible emergency funding.
